module_title: HTTP & API Design: REST, GraphQL & gRPC
description: HTTP semantics, REST principles, GraphQL schemas, gRPC Protocol Buffers, API Gateways, rate limiting, idempotency keys, and pagination.

topics.title: HTTP Methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE), Status Codes & Headers
topics.definition: The formal vocabulary and semantic rules of Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), governing how client-server systems request, mutate, delete, cache, and authenticate resources.
topics.why_we_need_it: Adhering to HTTP semantics ensures your API is predictable, cacheable by CDNs, safe from data corruption, and self-documenting across international engineering teams.
topics.real_world_analogy: Standard postal mail: HTTP Method is the action label (Return to sender, Certified delivery), Headers are the envelope stamps and return address, Status Codes are postal tracking confirmations (Delivered, Address not found, Returned).
topics.how_it_works:
HTTP Methods & Idempotence:

  • GET: Safe & Idempotent (Fetches resource without mutation). Cacheable!
  • POST: Unsafe & Non-Idempotent (Creates a new resource; calling 5 times creates 5 records).
  • PUT: Idempotent (Replaces entire resource; calling 5 times results in same state).
  • PATCH: Non-Idempotent / Partial Update (Mutates specific fields).
  • DELETE: Idempotent (Removes resource; calling 5 times produces same result).
conceptual_breakdown: 2xx Success: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content (Deletion success with empty body).
3xx Redirection: 301 Moved Permanently (SEO permanent redirect), 304 Not Modified (Conditional GET cache hit).
4xx Client Errors: 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (Missing auth), 403 Forbidden (Authenticated but lacking permissions), 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 429 Too Many Requests.
5xx Server Errors: 500 Internal Error, 502 Bad Gateway (Upstream crashed), 503 Service Unavailable (Overload/maintenance), 504 Gateway Timeout.

steps.description: 1. Client sends GET /product/42. Server returns JSON with 'ETag: 0xABCD12' and 'Cache-Control: max-age=3600'.
2. Client re-requests product later: sends 'If-None-Match: 0xABCD12' in request header.
3. Server checks hash: Product unchanged! Returns lightweight HTTP 304 Not Modified with ZERO response body bytes.

topics.tradeoffs: Using `PUT` requires the client to send the entire object payload (wasting bandwidth for 1-field changes). Using `PATCH` saves bandwidth by sending only changed fields (`{ "status": "shipped" }`) but requires complex partial update validation.

rows: Fetch headers only without body (Checking ETag / file size)

topics.failure_scenarios: Using `GET` for state-modifying actions (e.g. `GET /user/delete?id=5`): web crawlers, search indexing bots, and browser pre-fetching engines automatically trigger GET requests, unintentionally deleting entire databases.

common_mistakes.mistake: Returning HTTP 200 OK with an error body like `{ "status": "error", "code": 404 }`
common_mistakes.correction: Always use real HTTP status codes (e.g. 404, 401, 500). Proxies, CDNs, load balancers, and monitoring tools rely on true HTTP status codes for alerting and caching.

interview_questions.question: What is the difference between HTTP 401 Unauthorized and HTTP 403 Forbidden?
interview_questions.answer: HTTP 401 Unauthorized means authentication is missing or invalid (the server does not know who you are; provide a valid JWT/API key). HTTP 403 Forbidden means the server knows who you are, but you do not have permission to access that specific resource (RBAC authorization failure).

topics.title: Protocol Shootout: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC Trade-offs
topics.definition: The definitive technical comparison between the 3 major API paradigms: REST (Resource-oriented JSON over HTTP), GraphQL (Query-driven flexible client schemas), and gRPC (High-performance Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2).
topics.why_we_need_it: Choosing the wrong API protocol cripples performance: using REST for high-throughput internal microservices wastes CPU parsing ASCII JSON strings, while using gRPC for public web clients requires heavy browser proxy polyfills.
topics.real_world_analogy: REST is ordering a set combo meal from a menu; GraphQL is a custom salad bar where you pick the exact 3 ingredients you want; gRPC is a pneumatic tube delivering compressed military capsules at Mach 2.
topics.how_it_works:
REST: Resource URLs (`/users/42/posts`). Simple, universal, highly cacheable by CDNs, but suffers from Over-fetching (getting 50 fields when you need 1) and Under-fetching (requiring 5 sequential network calls to load 1 screen).

GraphQL: Single POST endpoint (`/graphql`). Client specifies exact fields needed in query body. Eliminates over/under-fetching, but prevents native CDN caching and risks complex nested N+1 database queries.

gRPC: Defines services in `.proto` files. Compiles into compact binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2 multiplexed streams. $7\times - 10\times$ faster serialization and $30\% - 50\%$ smaller payloads than JSON!
conceptual_breakdown: REST: Best for Public Developer APIs and standard CRUD web applications.
GraphQL: Best for Mobile Apps, complex analytics dashboards, and aggregating multi-service backends (Backend-For-Frontend / BFF pattern).
gRPC: Best for Internal East-West microservice communication, real-time streaming, and polyglot systems (C++, Go, Java, Python).

steps.description: Mobile App sends 1 GraphQL Query: 'query { user(id:1) { name, orders { id, total } } }'.
GraphQL Gateway parses AST and fires 2 parallel gRPC binary calls to User Service and Order Service.
Internal services respond via binary Protobuf in 1.5ms. Gateway combines data and returns clean JSON to mobile app.

topics.tradeoffs: GraphQL solves over-fetching but shifts query complexity to the backend; malicious users can submit 10-level deep nested queries that crash the database. Always enforce query depth limits and query cost analysis in GraphQL.

topics.failure_scenarios: The GraphQL N+1 Problem: fetching 100 users and their orders executes 1 query for users plus 100 individual queries for each user's orders (101 SQL queries total). Mitigation: Use Facebook's `DataLoader` pattern to batch and memoize database queries into a single `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (...)`.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using JSON REST for high-frequency internal microservice communication handling 100k QPS
common_mistakes.correction: Use gRPC for internal service-to-service communication. Parsing text JSON consumes up to 30% of CPU time at high throughput.

interview_questions.question: How do you explain the architectural decision of using GraphQL at the edge and gRPC internally?
interview_questions.answer: GraphQL is ideal for North-South client traffic because mobile devices over cellular connections need to fetch heterogeneous data in a single roundtrip without over-fetching. gRPC is ideal for East-West internal traffic because datacenter networks benefit from HTTP/2 multiplexing, binary serialization speed, and strict compile-time Protobuf typing.

topics.title: Pagination (Offset vs Cursor-based), Filtering, and Sorting Strategies
topics.definition: Techniques for querying and streaming large database result sets across API boundaries without exhausting database memory or suffering from the 'Missing/Duplicate Item' pagination bug.
topics.why_we_need_it: Returning 1,000,000 database rows in a single HTTP response crashes server memory and browser DOMs. Choosing between Offset and Cursor pagination determines whether query performance degrades as users scroll deeper.
topics.real_world_analogy: Offset pagination is counting 5,000 pages into a physical encyclopedia from Page 1 every single time; Cursor pagination is keeping a bookmark on the exact page you just read.
topics.how_it_works:
1. Offset-Based Pagination: Uses SQL LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000. The database must scan and discard the first 10,000 rows before returning 20. Performance degrades linearly ($O(N)$). Also causes duplicate/skipped items when new rows are inserted!

2. Cursor-Based Pagination (Keyset): Uses SQL WHERE id < 'last_seen_id' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20. The database jumps directly to the indexed cursor in $O(1)$ / $O(\log N)$ time. Infinite scroll stays lightning fast regardless of depth!
conceptual_breakdown: Offset Pagination: `GET /items?page=5&limit=20` • Good for static admin tables where jumping to a specific page (e.g. Page 12) is required.
Cursor Pagination: `GET /feed?cursor=eyJpZCI6MTAxfQ==&limit=20` • Standard for social feeds (Twitter, Instagram, Reddit, TikTok infinite scroll).
Cursor Structure: Base64-encoded string containing `(timestamp, id)` ensuring unique tie-breaking on identical timestamps.

steps.description: 2. Server queries DB: 'SELECT * FROM posts ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 10'. Returns posts + 'next_cursor: 1042'.
3. New post inserted at top by another user.
4. User scrolls: Client sends GET /api/v1/feed?cursor=1042&limit=10. Queries 'WHERE id < 1042'. Zero duplicate posts!

topics.tradeoffs: Cursor pagination delivers optimal $O(1)$ performance and prevents duplicate items, but prevents users from jumping directly to arbitrary page numbers (e.g. 'Jump to Page 45').

topics.failure_scenarios: The Offset Pagination Duplication Glitch: User is viewing Page 1 (Items 1-10). A new post is published at the top. User clicks Page 2 (`OFFSET 10`). Item #10 has now shifted to position #11, so the user sees Item #10 a second time on Page 2.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using `OFFSET 50000` on a table with 100 million rows
common_mistakes.correction: Never use large offsets on massive tables. Always adopt cursor-based pagination with indexed timestamp/ID compound keys.

interview_questions.question: How do you construct a tamper-proof cursor for cursor-based pagination with multiple sort fields (e.g. sort by likes, then by id)?
interview_questions.answer: Combine the sort fields into a tuple, serialize to JSON, and Base64-encode it: `base64_encode(JSON.stringify({ likes: 450, id: "post_992" }))`. In SQL, use row-value comparison: `WHERE (likes, id) < (450, 'post_992') ORDER BY likes DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20`.

topics.title: Idempotency Keys, Exponential Backoff Retries & API Gateway Routing
topics.definition: The reliability triad of distributed APIs: Idempotency Keys (guaranteeing that duplicate network requests execute exactly once), Exponential Backoff with Jitter (safe client retries), and API Gateway rate-limiting policies.
topics.why_we_need_it: Networks drop packets. If a mobile user clicks 'Pay $100' and the Wi-Fi disconnects after the server charges the card but before returning the HTTP 200 response, the mobile app retries. Without an idempotency key, the user is double-charged.
topics.real_world_analogy: An elevator call button: pressing the button 10 times in a row produces the exact same result as pressing it once (Idempotent).
topics.how_it_works:
Idempotency Key Workflow (Stripe Standard):

  1. Client generates a unique UUID (Idempotency-Key: 7b3e9...) and attaches it in HTTP header.
  2. Server receives request and attempts an atomic SET idempotency:7b3e9... IN_PROGRESS NX EX 120 in Redis.
  3. If key already exists with status COMPLETED, server skips execution and immediately returns the cached HTTP response from Redis!
  4. If key does not exist, server executes payment, stores final response in Redis, and returns HTTP 200.
conceptual_breakdown: Idempotency-Key Header: Client-generated UUID attached to unsafe `POST` requests.
Exponential Backoff: Retrying with exponentially increasing wait times ($T = 2^{\text{attempt}} \times 100\text{ms}$).
Full Jitter: Adding randomized noise to backoff ($T = \text{random}(0, 2^{\text{attempt}} \times 100\text{ms})$) to prevent the Thundering Herd retry storm.
API Gateway Rate Limiting: Enforces token-bucket rate limits returning `HTTP 429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After: 30` header.

steps.description: 1. Client submits POST /checkout with 'Idempotency-Key: UUID-99'. Initial payment charges $100.
2. Payment succeeds, response cached in Redis, but Wi-Fi drops before client receives ACK!
3. Client re-sends POST /checkout with identical 'Idempotency-Key: UUID-99'.
4. Gateway finds UUID-99 in Redis with status COMPLETED. Returns cached HTTP 200 instantly without re-charging card!

topics.tradeoffs: Retrying without jitter causes thousands of failed clients to retry at the exact same second (e.g. at $t=1\text{s}, t=2\text{s}, t=4\text{s}$), delivering a synchronized DDoS wave that crashes the recovering server.

comparison_matrix.title: Client Retry Strategies Comparison
rows: Moderate (Spreads attempts, but identical clients still pulse together)
Zero (Smooths retry traffic evenly over time spectrum)

topics.failure_scenarios: Double-Charging Bug: Mobile user taps 'Pay' twice during slow 3G connectivity. Without an idempotency key, the server processes two distinct database inserts, debiting the user's bank account twice.

common_mistakes.mistake: Generating the Idempotency Key on the server side
common_mistakes.correction: The Idempotency Key MUST be generated on the CLIENT side (in the mobile app/browser) BEFORE transmitting the first network request, so retries carry the identical key.

interview_questions.question: How do you implement an atomic idempotency check in distributed systems using Redis?
interview_questions.answer: Use Redis atomic command: `SET idempotency:<key> "IN_PROGRESS" NX EX 120`. 1. If return is `OK` (key was set), this is the first execution -> proceed to execute business logic. 2. When execution completes, update key with the response JSON: `SET idempotency:<key> "{\"status\":200,...}" EX 86400`. 3. If initial `SET NX` returned `nil` (key already exists), check its value: if still `IN_PROGRESS`, return HTTP 409 Conflict / 425 Too Early; if contains completed response, return cached response immediately.
